blocks.p: That moment when crying suddenly becomes uncontrollable, when your whole body shakes, your breathing becomes erratic, and you feel simultaneously vulnerable and powerful. If uncontrollable shaking when crying has happened to you, you may be experiencing something deeply biological and completely normal.
In fact, it's your nervous system doing exactly what it's designed to do.

You're not the only one. Therapy and coaching clients often bring this up, as well as podcast listeners. I'm going to address what typically happens when we cry, then what happens when we cry uncontrollably.
People report different types of experiences when they cry. There is no one way to cry that's best for all of us, like uncontrollable shakes, isolating in a bathroom, or even a destructive rage.
Crying is different for all of us, completely normal, and even possibly necessary as we climb the [Polyvagal ladder](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations). But why the shaking?

blocks.h: Why we cry and the Polyvagal Theory

blocks.p: Crying is a common and potentially therapeutic aspect of emotional release. Like when we grieve, or when we're letting go of some deep sadness. Crying often comes with it.
To understand why, it's important to understand what the Polyvagal ladder is and the function of crying.
The Polyvagal ladder is a metaphor for the mammalian autonomic nervous system from Deb Dana. There are three autonomic pathways in the ANS:

ul: ventral vagal social engagement system
sympathetic flight/fight system
[dorsal vagal immobilization system](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown)

blocks.p: The safety system at the top of the ladder, flight/fight in the middle, and shutdown at the bottom.
These three states have unique physiological, emotional, cognitive, and behavioral aspects.

ul: In the social engagement system, mammals impulsively connect. There may be an experience of calm, happiness, or belonging. Muscles relax while facial muscles show smiles, listening, surprise, and more.
In a flight/fight state, there is a tensing in preparation to mobilize the body to get to safety.
In shutdown, there is an emptiness as the body slows down to conserve resources in a possible death feign.

blocks.p: Two of these pathways can be active at the same time, something called a mixed state. You can learn a lot more about mixed states and the other fundamental Polyvagal Theory information on the [Polyvagal Intro page](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations). For now, let's focus on the mixed state of freeze.

blocks.h: Freeze of the autonomic nervous system

blocks.p: Freeze is a combination of shutdown and mobilization. The body is immobilized while in a fight-or-flight state.

blocks.h3: Freeze = immobilization + fight/flight activation happening simultaneously

blocks.p: Think about the last time you were in a dentist's chair. You may have had tense muscles, but were immobilized while a drill or pick was in your mouth. Your muscles are ready to run or fight, but your body is also immobilized. That's a minor example of the freeze mixed state.
[More about freeze](hub:freeze)

Of course, you can ultimately choose to get up and walk away. And there is an end to that experience. And you're not actually in significant danger. Once the procedure is done, you get up, make small talk, exchange smiles, and walk out into the sunlight outside. You're not traumatized, and the muscle activation you felt eases.
Now imagine that the tension in your muscles doesn't ease and becomes "frozen" in your body. That tension, the flight/fight activation, stays within the body.

The sympathetic activation is frozen in a specific moment in time and can be triggered by aspects of the event. Like, if you saw the dentist outside of the office, that flight/fight activation could resurface. Or if you heard one of the songs playing in the background during the procedure, it could be activating as well when you randomly hear it in the future. These are called "triggers," something that is very common in trauma.
Eventually, the frozen activation from the dentist's chair needs to be discharged.

When trauma occurs, that frozen activation can stay locked in your nervous system for months, years, or even decades. Your body remembers the threat, your muscles remember the tension, even when your thinking brain knows the danger has passed. That's not a character flaw; that's biology.

blocks.h: Why we shake when we cry

blocks.p: If we were wild animals, we would simply shake it off. Seriously. That's it. Wild animals are excellent at listening to their bodies' needs. If their body has a freeze experience, they shake it off. They shake and tremble, releasing the stuck state and returning to a self-regulated state. Peter Levine uses the example of a polar bear that, after being chased and tranquilized, shakes and trembles as it comes to, and is not traumatized.
Of course, humans are animals still. We still retain the capacity to shake off stuck traumatic energy.

Humans make things much more complex in the process, like shaming and guilt-tripping ourselves. And the traumatic events we endure are much more complex than the survive-or-die variety that wild animals endure.

Our traumatic events often include things like rejection, shame, humiliation, deception, and more. Things that animals don't do to each other. There are layers to our traumas, oftentimes generational.
So simply shaking it off isn't really a practical option for us, at least, not all at once.
This is compounded by the fact that we also keep ourselves stuck in traumatized states. We tell ourselves reinforcing stories, like "I shouldn't have been there" or "I deserved it."
[More about how your nervous system works](hub:found)

Shaking and trembling are best for stuck shock trauma that comes from a freeze state. I haven't found it all that useful for returning sympathetic energy, like for someone coming out of a [stuck shutdown state](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown). Instead of shaking it off, that person needs to welcome the sympathetic activation back into the system.

Regardless of all this, human beings do nevertheless shake off their frozen energy. It's called crying. At least, it could look like crying. We can definitely do the polar bear-type shaking, but we typically don't. (I consider that more of a "pure" or first-level form of trauma releasing.)
Like I said at the outset, crying is "an aspect of emotional releasing." But it's not just emotionally releasing something; there is an autonomic shift happening. Stuck frozen energy is discharging.

Think about it, when humans cry, we go through physiological shifts, just like the polar bear. Breathing spontaneously changes, from heavier to lighter. There is a tensing of our muscles and often full-body heaves. We tighten and constrict. Fluid discharges from our eyes. Our awareness goes from highly constricted and narrow to fuller. And we may even have an impulse to connect with another during or after a cry. Really, we shake and tremble. It's a full-body release of stuck frozen energy.
If done successfully.

If you can cry successfully, it eventually stops. Eventually, there is an ease in breathing and a return to being grounded in the present moment. I often see my therapy clients do some crying and then shift into laughter as their autonomic nervous system climbs into a state of safety and social engagement. For the person grieving in sadness, it turns into appreciation, and a pleasant memory comes to their mind.
Crying is a normal and maybe even necessary part of this autonomic shift.

blocks.h: How to support yourself when shaking and crying

blocks.p: Now that you understand why shaking happens when you cry, here's what you can actually do about it. The goal isn't to stop the shaking, remember, that's your nervous system discharging. The goal is to create safety so your system can complete the release and return to grounding.
These techniques help you stay present and regulated during the emotional release:

ol: Use top-down cognitions to permit your experience
Continually reconnect with your breath as needed

blocks.p: If you feel crying coming on, take a moment to anchor yourself in your body and your environment:

ul: Extended exhale: Some like controlled breathing methods. I recommend one intentional, bigger breath in and out in whatever way feels best. For the most part, try and connect with the natural in and out of your breath.

Use your senses: Listen to the sounds around you. Notice what your eye is pulled toward. And feel the texture of something enjoyable. You can also use scent with a candle. Taste is a possibility, but typically less so.
Feel your feet: Press them firmly into the ground. Notice the weight and pressure.

blocks.why: Grounding in safety first is what lets a release complete. This practice is that grounding, tuned to you.

blocks.p: [More about safety](hub:safety)
As you cry, your thoughts might wander toward judgment or wondering if you're crying correctly. Don't fight your thoughts. Instead, try to focus on a couple cognitive skills:

ol: Validate your experience: just acknowledge and name what you're going through.
Normalize your experience: does it make sense you're having this experience? Of course, it does.
Give yourself permission: explicitly tell yourself it's okay to cry, sob, shake, and tremble.
Remind yourself you're literally safe: it doesn't hurt to remind yourself that you're safe and you're in no actual threat.

blocks.p: These top-down cognitions can help you reground yourself without fighting your thoughts.

blocks.prompt: Write the words you would want to hear the next time a big cry comes. ("It's okay to cry...")

blocks.p: The one, intentional breath from before is not a one-time thing. As you cry, continually check your breath. Your body will spontaneously breathe and take care of you. There's no need to change it.
But if you like, it's completely okay to do another intentional breath as a way to re-anchor yourself in the present.
Same thing, bigger breath on the way in, slower on the way out if comfortable.

The bottom line: Shaking and trembling when crying are not emergencies. They're releases. By creating conditions of safety, through grounding, cognitions, and breath, you allow your nervous system to do what it evolved to do: return to regulation.
Once the shaking and crying naturally subside, give yourself time to recover. Ultimately, listen to your body's needs, but here are some potentially helpful pointers:

ul: Gentle movement: Slow stretching, walking, or swaying
Hydration: Drink water, your body has been working hard
Connect with nature: Look out a window, step outside, or listen to the world around you
Connection: If safe, be near someone you trust, or reach out to a friend, or connect with your pet

blocks.p: These practices signal to your nervous system: "You're safe now. The release is complete."

Yes, absolutely. Shaking when crying is a completely normal physiological response. When you cry, your nervous system is actively releasing stored emotional and physical tension. The shaking you experience is your body's way of discharging that activation, it's not a sign something is wrong with you.

In fact, if you can cry and shake without judgment, you're allowing your nervous system to do exactly what it evolved to do: process and release. The problem isn't the shaking; the problem is when we shame ourselves for it and try to suppress it.

blocks.h3: When should I see a doctor about shaking when crying?

blocks.p: While shaking when crying is normal, there are situations where it's worth consulting a healthcare provider:

ul: If the shaking is severe or uncontrollable and happens even when you're not crying
If it's accompanied by other symptoms like chest pain, difficulty breathing, or dizziness
If you're concerned about an underlying medical condition (thyroid issues, neurological conditions, or medication side effects can sometimes cause tremors)

blocks.p: For medical evaluation of tremors, the [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/tremor) and [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/) have excellent resources on when shaking warrants a doctor's visit. Your therapist or primary care doctor can help determine if your shaking has a medical component to address.

From a Polyvagal perspective, if your shaking is tied to emotional release and trauma processing, that's actually a good sign, it means your nervous system is working. But if you're concerned, it never hurts to get a professional medical opinion.

blocks.h3: Can medication cause shaking when crying?

blocks.p: MedlinePlus says yes, [certain medications can cause or worsen tremors](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000765.htm). If you're taking medications and notice new or increased shaking when crying (or at other times), it's worth discussing with your prescribing doctor.
Common medication classes that can cause tremors include:

ul: Some antidepressants
Stimulant medications
Corticosteroids
Certain asthma medications

blocks.p: This is a medical question, so I'd recommend checking with your doctor or pharmacist if you suspect your medication is contributing. They can assess whether it's a side effect that needs adjustment or if it's unrelated to your medication.
From a nervous system perspective, emotional shaking during crying is different from medication-induced tremors, but a healthcare provider can help you distinguish between the two.

blocks.h3: What's the difference between anxiety shaking and shaking when crying?

blocks.p: Great question, these are actually different nervous system states, even though they both involve shaking.

Anxiety shaking happens when your sympathetic nervous system (fight/flight) is activated by perceived threat or worry. Your body is preparing to act, but the activation gets stuck. The shaking feels jittery, uncontrolled, and often accompanied by racing thoughts. Although I'm calling it "anxiety shaking," it can also involve fear or anger.

Shaking when crying is different. It's your nervous system releasing activation. You're moving through an emotional experience, and the shaking is part of the discharge process. It often feels cathartic, like your body is letting something go. After the cry, you typically feel calmer and more grounded.
Think of it this way:

ul: Anxiety shaking = activation building up (sympathetic dominant)
Crying shakes = activation being released (moving toward regulation)

blocks.p: Both involve shaking, but in different directions. One is your nervous system maybe stuck; the other is your nervous system releasing stuckness.

blocks.h3: How long does shaking when crying last?

blocks.p: It varies. Some people shake for just a few seconds or minutes during a cry. Others experience shaking for 5 to 15 minutes as part of a deeper emotional release.

There's no "right" duration. Your nervous system will shake for as long as it needs to discharge the activation. The key is to not interrupt it. Let the shaking happen. Don't try to control it or make it stop.
Once the shaking subsides naturally, you'll typically notice:

ul: Deeper, easier breathing
A sense of calm or relief
Feeling more grounded in your body
Sometimes even laughter or a shift in mood

blocks.p: If you're concerned that shaking is lasting an unusually long time or feels uncontrollable, that's worth checking in with a healthcare provider. But in most cases, letting the shaking run its course is exactly what your nervous system needs.
